summary:
VERGE (Verified Evidence and Risk-Governed Exploration) is an interactive scientific research prototype designed to make NASA microgravity combustion data easier to explore, understand, and verify.

Developed for the Flame in Freefall challenge, VERGE addresses a critical problem: scientific results can be misinterpreted when separated from their experimental conditions, measurement units, and original sources.

Built with Python and Streamlit, VERGE combines source-linked search, explainable ranking, structured claim verification, and traceable evidence records. It uses selected NASA FLEX and BASS-II combustion research to demonstrate how scientific claims can be checked against original experimental reports. An optional Google Gemini integration provides AI-generated candidate interpretations while clearly distinguishing them from independently verified results.

VERGE emphasizes scientific transparency, reproducibility, and responsible AI use. Rather than presenting AI-generated explanations as established facts, it preserves evidence, highlights uncertainties, and explicitly identifies limitations.

The project provides a foundation for more reliable AI-assisted scientific research and future analysis of complex experimental data relevant to space exploration.
details:
VERGE (Verified Evidence and Risk-Governed Exploration) is an interactive scientific research prototype developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Flame in Freefall. Its purpose is to help users explore microgravity combustion research while preserving the evidence, experimental conditions, and limitations behind scientific claims.

How it works

VERGE provides a structured workflow for exploring NASA research, inspecting source-linked data, and verifying specific scientific statements. Its public, bilingual dashboard includes six sections: Overview, Explore, Search, Verify, Evidence Ledger, and Methods & Limitations.

Users can explore experimental records, inspect original NASA references, search selected FLEX data through explainable lexical ranking, and submit structured claims for deterministic verification. The system checks supported source values, units, and scope restrictions, returning verdicts such as SUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED, INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE, or OUT_OF_SCOPE. Results include explanations and traceable evidence references.

Scientific foundations

The prototype uses two NASA investigations: FLEX (PSI-69), studying liquid-fuel droplet combustion, and BASS-II (PSI-25), studying solid-fuel combustion.

The current scientific release contains 17 selected FLEX records, including 10 records verified for limited source inspection and seven requiring further review. BASS-II contributes two oxygen-condition rows containing six method-specific experimental, computational, and theoretical values.

VERGE preserves original values, measurement units, source locations, and quality restrictions. Project-specific NASA-DAP and NASA-EVP protocols guide data auditing and structured claim verification. Unresolved discrepancies are explicitly flagged rather than silently corrected.

Artificial intelligence and creativity

VERGE combines deterministic scientific verification with an optional Google Gemini interpretation module. Gemini generates candidate explanations from a small set of selected, source-linked evidence snippets. Its outputs are marked CANDIDATE_NOT_VERIFIED because citation and format checks do not establish scientific correctness.

The Gemini source code is publicly available on GitHub, while live generation is restricted to a locally launched version requiring a user-provided API key.

The project's distinctive approach is to separate AI-generated interpretation from verified evidence, making uncertainty and scientific boundaries visible instead of presenting fluent AI responses as established conclusions.

Technology and development

VERGE was developed primarily in Python using Streamlit, Pandas, Plotly, Pytest, and Git/GitHub. It runs as a publicly accessible web application, with a separate Windows launcher for prepared local environments. No specialized computing hardware is required for its deterministic functionality.

The project was developed by one human participant with AI assistance during research, programming, testing, and documentation.

The latest independent project audit recorded 237 passing software tests and 28 passing predefined structured scientific verification cases.

Benefits and intended impact

VERGE aims to make scientific research more transparent, reproducible, and accessible to students, researchers, and engineers. Key development priorities included source traceability, scientific accuracy, reproducibility, responsible AI use, and clear communication of limitations.

VERGE does not predict spacecraft fires, certify safety, or extrapolate experimental findings to lunar or Martian gravity. Future development will focus on expanding audited NASA data coverage and improving independent verification of AI-generated scientific claims.
